title: Turn a research paper into a short talk
objective: Select the question, evidence and main message of a study.

slides.title: Choose a small research story
body: Start with the question the authors tried to answer. Choose a result that helps answer it.
Explain why that result matters. Keep one important limit of the study.

slides.title: Make four speaking notes
body: Classroom example: a class counted 7 insects on yellow flowers and 3 on white flowers in one garden visit.
Question: Which flowers had more visiting insects? Evidence: 7 and 3.
Message: More insects visited the yellow flowers on this visit. Limit: one visit.

slides.title: Read the first case together
body: Report: A class asked which pond had more frogs. It counted nine at the large pond and four at the small pond on one morning. The team wants to visit again.

slides.title: Try it with a partner
body: Give the main question in one sentence.
Make three short notes for a talk: question, result, next step.
Ask which place had more animals.

slides.title: Try a new case
body: Report: A class asked which garden had more bees. It counted twelve in the flower garden and five in the herb garden on one morning. The team wants to visit again.

slides.title: Work on your own
body: Give the main question in one sentence.
Make three short notes for a talk: question, result, next step.
Tell your partner the main message in two sentences. Include one limit.

slides.title: Rehearse with fewer notes
body: Write four key words. Speak from those notes. Ask your partner to repeat your main message.
